title: Japanese Motor Market
oneLine: A live marketplace for Japanese cars, bootstrapped by a data pipeline I built to scrape, structure and load real auction listings.

specs.Role: Solo: scraper, seed pipeline, web app, deployment
specs.Pipeline: Python scraper, TypeScript seed and repair scripts
specs.Stack: Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, Prisma, Postgres on Neon
specs.Services: Clerk for auth, Cloudflare Images, deployed on Vercel with a custom domain

intake.question: What is it, in one sentence?
intake.hint: Correct my sentence if I got the product wrong.
intake.draft: A marketplace for Japanese cars, backed by a Python scraper that pulls completed Bring a Trailer auctions through the same public WordPress REST endpoint the site itself calls when you click Show More.

intake.question: Role, timeline, status
intake.draft: READ THIS BEFORE THE PAGE SHIPS. The repo is 7 commits, all on 7 May 2026, and its first commit is "Initial JMM scaffold from CMM". Its own CLAUDE.md says it was forked from Classic Motor Market in May 2026, and the 20,245 listings come from a sibling Python project called japanese-scrapper that is not among the repos I can see. As written, this page invites "tell me about building Japanese Motor Market" and the true answer is a one day rebrand of another site of yours. The stronger and more honest framing is the opposite one: Classic Motor Market is the real build, 36 commits and 104 TypeScript files from November 2025 to April 2026, and JMM is the evidence you could retarget it to a new market in a day, stripping the whole Stripe and membership layer and swapping NextAuth for Clerk on the way. That is a better engineering story than the listing count. NEEDS YOU: confirm the scraper is yours, and decide which of the two sites gets the featured slot.

intake.question: What made it hard?
intake.hint: Pick one of my candidates or replace them.
intake.draft: Candidates I can see from the code: your scraper has random delays, certifi handling and retry logic, which means Bring a Trailer fought you. Or it is the data model, since you carry 12 models including ads, events and blog posts. Or pulling comparable pricing out of unstructured listing text. Which one actually cost you nights?

intake.question: What did you decide, and what did you reject?
intake.hint: Why the REST endpoint over HTML parsing.
intake.draft: You went after the WP REST endpoint instead of parsing rendered HTML. That is the decision, and HTML scraping is the alternative you rejected. Say why in your own words, because the reasoning is the interesting part.

intake.question: What number can you put on it?
intake.hint: Add anything I could not see: users, traffic, cars listed by real people.
intake.draft: From the repo: 20,245 listings scraped, 27 fields per listing, 50 image sets pulled, 12 data models, plus a separate dataset from a year earlier for comparison. Twenty thousand listings is a genuinely strong number. Lead with it.

intake.question: What broke, and what did you do?
intake.hint: The scraper failure that made you write the retry logic.
intake.draft: Rate limits, SSL, a schema change on their side, or bad rows. That retry logic in scrape.py exists for a reason. What was it?

intake.question: What media do you have?
intake.hint: What you have, and whether you will make the chart.
intake.draft: NEEDS YOU: screenshots of the listings page and the admin dashboard, and the scraper running. But the real opportunity is a chart. You have 20k listings and a year-over-year set. One good chart of Japanese car values over time would be the most interesting single object on your entire site.

intake.question: What would you do differently?
intake.hint: Two sentences. Not self criticism, a design judgement you would make differently now.

intro: Japanese Motor Market is a free-to-list marketplace for JDM and Japanese-made vehicles in the US. Sellers sign up and post a vehicle through a five-step wizard with photo upload. Buyers browse, save listings to a watchlist and contact sellers directly. There are no fees or commissions.
It has two parts. The first is a data pipeline that collects real auction listings and turns them into structured marketplace records. The second is the production web app those records load into.
This is data engineering plus a shipped product. There is no trained model and no LLM feature in it today. The parsing is rule-based, and the model work is listed at the end as planned, not built.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: An empty marketplace cannot be designed or tested
body: A new marketplace starts with no listings. Without listings there is nothing to lay out, nothing to search and nothing to test against.
I solved the cold start by building a pipeline that collects real auction listings and turns them into typed marketplace records.

sections.label: Pipeline
sections.title: The data pipeline
body: A Python scraper collects listings and images. A TypeScript seed script parses the text into typed rows and loads them into Postgres and Cloudflare Images. The live site reads from there.

flow.summary: The scraper pages through a Bring a Trailer REST endpoint and fetches each listing page. It writes raw JSON, clean JSON and CSV, plus the images. A TypeScript seed script parses and structures those records, then loads typed rows into Postgres and tagged images into Cloudflare Images, which the live site reads.

boxes.title: REST endpoint

sections.label: Collection
sections.title: Calling the endpoint the site calls
body: Bring a Trailer category pages paginate through an undocumented WordPress REST endpoint. The scraper calls that endpoint directly instead of parsing rendered HTML. It then fetches each listing page for the description, the curated gallery images at full resolution and the essentials sidebar: seller, location, chassis and detail bullets.

The scraper is 540 lines of Python with no requests, no BeautifulSoup and no headless browser. Every network call retries with exponential backoff, honours Retry-After on HTTP 429, and waits between calls.

A time-window mode walks back through pages to sample listings older than N days. I used it to pull two cohorts: the newest listings, and listings from a year or more ago. That way the dataset is not just one week of the market.

facts.CSV: A flattened version of the same records
facts.Raw JSON: The untouched API payload, so new fields can be derived later without re-scraping

sections.label: Parsing
sections.title: From auction text to typed rows
body: A 384-line TypeScript seed script turns the auction text into database rows. It pulls year, make and model out of free-form titles, reads mileage out of the description, fills in location, and maps the detail bullets into structured fields.
This is rule-based: regex plus a known-makes list. A title with no known make gets a null make and model, not a guess.

sections.label: Loading
sections.title: Loading, and one repair
body: Images are uploaded to Cloudflare Images with two metadata tags, project and source. That keeps seeded, repaired and user-uploaded images separable.

After the first load I found a data-quality bug: the scraper had skipped each listing's cover photo. I wrote a repair script that fetches the cover and adds it. The repair is idempotent. It marks the rows it has fixed, so it is safe to run again.

sections.label: App
sections.title: The app
body: The app has a listing catalog and detail pages with galleries, a five-step sell wizard with drag-to-reorder photo upload and zod validation, a watchlist, contact-seller and report flows, account pages, and an admin area for users, listings, events and ad slots.

I forked the codebase from an earlier marketplace of mine and moved auth from NextAuth to Clerk. I wrote a small shim that keeps the old auth() interface, creates the database user on first sign-in, and adopts pre-seeded accounts by email match. The rest of the app did not have to change.
sections.callout: Demo listings are seeded from public auction data. The photos and descriptions come from completed Bring a Trailer auctions, and the seller names are fictional.

sections.label: Known issue
sections.title: What is wrong in the demo data today
body: The mileage rule has a bug. When a description gives mileage in the short form, such as "55k miles", the rule reads it as 55. So many demo listings show a mileage that is a thousand times too low. The listing below shows 19 miles. The source listing says about 19k.

Some fields are placeholders. The auction data has no condition grade, title status or listing date, so the seed script fills those with random values to make the demo look like a marketplace. When no mileage or price can be read, it fills those the same way.
Fixing the mileage rule and re-running the seed comes before any of the planned work below.

sections.label: Agent
sections.title: Building with an AI agent
body: I built this with Claude Code as a coding agent. Each of the two sub-projects has a CLAUDE.md file that documents the architecture decisions, the gotchas and the open work, so the agent and I pick up with the same context each session.
This is a different skill from training models. It is directing AI tooling on a real codebase and keeping it accountable.
